name: Recall bias
statement: Recall bias is the error that arises when people who have suffered an outcome remember or report past exposures differently from people who have not.
meaning: This is a property of a measurement rather than a habit of a mind, which it shares with selection bias, entry 82, and with little else in this collection. It appears wherever exposure is measured by asking people to remember, and where having the disease changes what they say. The distinction that carries all the weight is between differential and non-differential error. If cases and controls misreport at the same rate, the misclassification is non-differential, and it usually drags an estimate towards no effect. If cases misreport at a different rate, the estimate can move in either direction, and an association can be created where none exists. Swan, Shaw and Schulman showed that this kind of reporting bias, and the selection bias introduced by the usual remedy for it, are both "algebraically equivalent to bias arising from exposure misclassification". Detecting it needs a gold standard, meaning a record made before the outcome was known and held against what the respondent says afterwards. Coughlin's review drew the line the term keeps losing, that "a distinction must be drawn between recall which is biased and that which is simply inaccurate".

origin.note: "Bias in analytic research", Journal of Chronic Diseases 32(1-2), 51 to 63, which prints "a first draft of a catalog of biases which may distort the design, execution, analysis and interpretation of research". Recall bias is the eighth bias discussed in the body and item (k) under measurement in the appendix. Sackett coins no term and credits no one, and his worked example comes from Klemetti and Saxén in 1967. The first journal article devoted to recall bias alone is Raphael's four-page piece in the International Journal of Epidemiology in 1987, whose text was not obtained for this entry.

evidence: Sackett's own example is a Finnish validation study. Mothers were interviewed during pregnancy and again after delivery, and Sackett reports that 28 per cent of mothers whose pregnancies had ended in fetal death or malformation, against 20 per cent of matched mothers whose pregnancies ended normally, "reported exposure to drugs which could not be substantiated either in earlier prospective interviews or in other health records". Those two figures are quoted here from Sackett's page, not from Klemetti and Saxén, whose 1967 paper is held at PubMed Central as page images only and was not obtained. Werler, Pober, Nelson and Holmes built the first test designed for the question. They interviewed mothers after delivery at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston during 1984 and compared what they said with exposures documented in obstetric records during the pregnancy. Their measure, relative sensitivity, is the ratio of reporting accuracy for mothers of malformed infants to that of mothers of nonmalformed infants. Across eight exposures it ran from 0.8 for nausea or vomiting to 7.6 for use of birth control after conception, with 2.7 for urinary tract or yeast infection, 1.4 for a history of infertility, 1.2 for antibiotic or antifungal drug use, 1.2 for spotting or bleeding, 1.1 for elective abortion history and 1.0 for any over-the-counter drug use. The largest test is Hungarian. Rockenbauer, Olsen, Czeizel, Pedersen and Sørensen compared self-reported drug intake with medically notified intake in the Hungarian Case-Control Surveillance System of Congenital Abnormalities, which holds 22,865 cases with congenital abnormalities and 39,151 controls. Recall error was present, worst for drugs taken briefly, and cases placed the timing of intake slightly closer to the interview than controls did. Their conclusion is that a surveillance system of this type "may frequently cause spurious associations, with biased odds ratios up to a factor of 1.9". Severity or visibility of the abnormality made no difference to it. Infante-Rivard and Jacques found the bias switching on and off within one study. Working inside a Quebec case-control study of childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, they checked reported distance from home to power lines against measured distance. Sensitivity was 62 per cent among cases living in an area where an excess of the disease was perceived and blamed on power lines. For other cases it was 35 per cent, against 36 per cent for hospital controls and 22 per cent for population controls. For reported prenatal radiographic examinations, sensitivity was 64 per cent for cases and 71 per cent for population controls. Non-differential recall error can be large on its own. Brusco and Watts held self-reported general practitioner visits from 751 rehabilitation patients, mean age 74, against national insurer claims, and found under-reporting of 14 per cent across twelve months, made up of over-reporting by 35 per cent in the first six months and under-reporting by 36 per cent in the second.

replication.headline: The same validation design has been run in several fields and the answers disagree; INTERPHONE checked recalled mobile phone use against operator records for 212 cases and 296 controls and found the two groups off by the same factors.
replication.detail: Recall bias is testable in a way selection bias is not, because a record made before the outcome was known can be held against what people say afterwards. That test has been run repeatedly and does not give one answer. Vrijheid and colleagues collected mobile phone records from network operators in three INTERPHONE countries, covering an average of two years, for 212 brain tumour cases and 296 controls, and compared them with use reported at interview. Mean ratios of reported to recorded use were the same for both groups, understating the number of calls by a factor of 0.81 and overstating call duration by a factor of 1.4. Their verdict is that "there was little evidence for differential recall errors overall or in recent time periods", with the qualification that ratios rose with time before interview for cases and not for controls, on few subjects. Khoury, James and Erickson reached a similar place from data rather than records. They compared odds ratios for ten defect and risk-factor pairs in an Atlanta case-control study of 4,918 babies with serious defects and 3,029 babies without, using affected and normal controls in turn, and report that "in all instances, the use of affected controls did not change etiologic inferences derived from using normal controls". They conclude that "concerns about recall bias are overrated in birth defects studies". Werler and colleagues, Rockenbauer and colleagues, and Infante-Rivard and Jacques in one subgroup found the opposite. The pattern that fits all of them is that differential recall appears where the exposure is salient, rare or publicly blamed, and not otherwise, which is a weaker claim than the term as usually used implies.

limits: There is no effect size for recall bias. Each validation study measures one exposure, in one population, against one kind of record, and the figures do not travel: 7.6 for birth control after conception in Boston in 1984 says nothing about how a Hungarian mother recalls a course of antibiotics. Searches of PubMed, Crossref and the open web in August 2026 for a pooled estimate across validation studies returned none. The nearest thing found is Chouinard and Walter, who collected the sixteen case-control studies published between 1966 and 1990 that applied a validated gold standard equally to cases and controls, and reported correlations between case and control data quality of 0.81 on crude agreement, 0.78 on kappa, 0.58 on sensitivity and 0.62 on specificity. They found no relationship between the absolute difference in agreement and the overall level of agreement, which contradicts Coughlin's suggestion that recall bias is worse where recall is poor in general. Differential error may also be the smaller problem. Vrijheid and colleagues ran Monte Carlo simulations inside INTERPHONE using recall error values taken from validation studies, and found that random errors at plausible levels can produce a large underestimate of risk, that random errors mattered more than plausible systematic errors, and that "differential errors in recall had very little additional impact in the presence of large random errors". The standard remedy carries its own cost. Drews, Greenland and Flanders worked through the algebra for a case-control study of sudden infant death syndrome and found that "even when recall bias exists, the observed association can be closer to the true association when a population control series is used than when a restricted-control group is used".
misreadings: Sackett's definition is not the one the term now carries. His entry reads in full: "Recall bias. Questions about specific exposures may be asked several times of cases but only once of controls." That is a fault in the interviewing, not in the memory. The mechanism modern epidemiology means by recall bias is catalogued three items above it, as underlying cause bias or rumination bias, where "cases may ruminate about possible causes for their illnesses" and so report their past differently. Sackett cross-references the two and keeps them apart. The second error is treating any inaccuracy of memory as recall bias. Brusco and Watts found patients out by a third in both directions inside one year, and error of that kind, if it falls equally on cases and controls, moves an estimate towards the null rather than away from it. The third error is confusing it with telescoping, entry 236, which is a claim about dating rather than about who reports what. A respondent who misplaces a real event in time is telescoping; a mother who reports a drug that no record supports is the case Sackett described. The fourth is treating the label as a finding. Naming recall bias establishes that an association might have been manufactured, and Khoury and colleagues found that switching to affected controls left all ten of their inferences intact, so the direction and the size still have to be argued from data. The fifth is assuming the fix is free, when Swan, Shaw and Schulman showed that comparing two malformed groups replaces one bias with another and that "the choice of study design involves balancing these two sources of bias".
